themes.theme: Model contract terms for the AI supply chain
themes.definition: Template contract terms or clauses that an EU body offers, or points to, for agreements between AI providers and their suppliers, or between public buyers and AI providers.
themes.what_is_set_out: EU046 (the AI Act, from its article numbering [inference]) lets the AI Office develop and recommend voluntary model terms for contracts between providers of high-risk AI systems and the third parties that supply them with tools, services, components or processes; the coder notes that the terms are to be published free of charge in an easily usable electronic format and should take account of sector-specific contractual requirements. Recital 90 gives the same offer to 'the Commission' with 'could', and Article 25(4) to 'the AI Office' with 'may', so even the operative text leaves it optional whether the terms are written at all. These terms govern the provider's own supply chain, not the contract between a public body and the provider [inference]. The EDPS orientations on generative AI (EDPS_GenAI_orientations) point EU institutions, 'as an example', to model contractual clauses for the procurement of AI by public organisations, developed through the Commission's 'Procurement of AI Community', and to standard contractual clauses between controllers and processors, whose issuer the passage does not name. No passage in this group says what any of these clauses should contain about testing, accuracy, model versions or access to a tool's outputs.
themes.holders: The Commission (Recital 90) and the AI Office (Art. 25(4)) as possible developers of voluntary model terms; the European Commission through its 'Procurement of AI Community' initiative; the issuer of the controller-processor clauses is not stated.
themes.binding: Discretionary throughout: 'could' (recital) and 'may' (article) for whether the terms are developed, and the terms themselves are 'voluntary'. The EDPS passages present clauses only as an example or as something 'relevant to consider'. Nothing is said to follow if the terms are not developed or not used.

quotes.quote: The AI Office may develop and recommend voluntary model terms for contracts between providers of high-risk AI systems and third parties that supply tools, services, components or processes
the European Commission, through the “Procurement of AI Community” initiative, has brought together relevant stakeholders in procuring AI solutions to develop wid e model contractual clauses
It is also relevant to consider the standard contractual clauses between controllers and processors under the Regulation

themes.theme: Guidance and best practice for public procurement of AI
themes.definition: Guidelines, best-practice work and programmes meant to help public bodies buy AI from suppliers (a split of the starting code 'supplier contracts').
themes.what_is_set_out: EU046 is the only binding text in this group that speaks to public buyers: Article 62(3)(d) gives the AI Office the task to 'evaluate and promote the convergence of best practices in public procurement procedures in relation to AI systems', and Recital 143 says the Commission should do the same; neither gives content, a deadline or an output for that work. The JRC report JRC129100 says more about substance but only as recommendation: EU-level procurement guidelines that give 'directions and criteria' for national guidelines, multilingual sets of guidelines developed with Member States' national procurement authorities, and guideline content that empowers procurers and helps them 'mitigate common risks and obstacles'. It cites procurement guidelines already issued by international organisations (the coder notes the World Economic Forum among them, a non-state source) and expects the Commission's Adopt AI programme to 'play a crucial role' in facilitating AI procurement in the public sector (the coder notes the report elsewhere describes it as financing AI procurement). Neither document, in these passages, says which risks the guidance should address or what it should require of suppliers about testing, accuracy, documentation or access to outputs. One coder placed passage 027 in Decision-making/Design, reading 'directions and criteria' as standard-setting.
themes.holders: The AI Office (Art. 62(3)(d)) and the Commission (Recital 143). In JRC129100 the author of the guidelines is mostly not stated; national procurement authorities are named as partners, procurers and civil servants as recipients, and international organisations and the Commission's Adopt AI programme as existing sources.
themes.binding: Art. 62(3)(d) is a statutory task of the AI Office, but the verb is 'promote' and no consequence is stated; the recital uses 'should'. JRC129100 uses 'should provide', 'This calls for actions' and 'There is therefore a clear need to': recommendations with no named holder and no consequence. The Adopt AI and international-organisation passages are mentions of resources, not offers made by the document.

quotes.quote: evaluate and promote the convergence of best practices in public procurement procedures in relation to AI systems.
Develop and align procurement guidelines at the EU level , providing directions and criteria for developing national guidelines in compliance with EU principles and regulations.
Develop multilingual sets of AI procurement guidelines in partnership with the national procurement authorities of the EU Member States.

Procurement guidelines should provide information on how to facilitate public procurement processes, empowering procurers and providing guidance on how to mitigate common risks and obstacles when procuring AI.

themes.theme: Shared electronic tools for notification and reporting
themes.definition: Electronic tools, platforms or databases, provided by an EU body, through which authorities send notifications or reports to one another.
themes.what_is_set_out: Under Article 30(2) of EU046, notifying authorities must notify the Commission and the other Member States of each conformity assessment body 'using the electronic notification tool developed and managed by the Commission'; the coder notes the same tool is used for changes to notifications (Art. 36(1)). Passage 009 is a fragment of the same sentence as passage 010. The Omnibus (EU_Omnibus), in its replacement of Article 30(2), keeps exactly this wording, so the tool survives the amendment. ENISA's paper on frontier AI (ENISA_frontier) points to the Cyber Resilience Act's Single Reporting Platform and the EU Vulnerability Database as able to 'help support' some of its recommendations, without naming their operator (the coder infers ENISA). These tools carry information about conformity assessment bodies and about software vulnerabilities; none in this group carries information about a public body's use of an AI tool or about how a tool performs [inference].
themes.holders: The Commission develops and manages the notification tool; Member States' notifying authorities must use it. The operator of the Single Reporting Platform and the EU Vulnerability Database is not stated.
themes.binding: Use of the notification tool is mandatory for notifying authorities ('shall notify ... using'), in both the original and the Omnibus text; the Commission's provision of the tool is stated as fact. The ENISA passage says only that existing platforms 'can help'. No consequence for failure is stated.

quotes.quote: Notifying authorities shall notify the Commission and the other Member States, using the electronic notification tool developed and managed by the Commission, of each conformity assessment body referred to in paragraph 1.

quotes.location: Art. 1(16), replacing AI Act Art. 30(2); p. 21
quotes.quote: using the electronic notification tool developed and managed by the Commission
The CRA’s Single Reporting Platform (SRP) and EU Vulnerability Database (EUVD) can help support the operationalisation of some of these recommendations.

themes.theme: Advice channels and contact points for deployers, SMEs and local public authorities
themes.definition: Channels, interfaces or standing invitations through which actors can put questions to authorities and receive advice on applying the rules.
themes.what_is_set_out: Article 62(1)(c) of EU046 requires Member States to use existing dedicated channels, and where appropriate set up new ones, to communicate with SMEs, start-ups, deployers, other innovators and, 'as appropriate, local public authorities', so as to advise them and answer queries about implementing the Regulation; Recital 143 says the same with 'should' and, per the coder, asks Member States to work together for consistency. Article 57(17) requires the Commission to build a single interface holding all relevant information on AI regulatory sandboxes, through which stakeholders can interact with sandboxes and raise enquiries with competent authorities and, per the coder, seek non-binding guidance on conformity. The guidelines on general-purpose AI models (EU088) invite providers to contact the AI Office 'immediately and proactively', describing the Office as dedicated to supporting providers in complying. Public bodies appear only as deployers or, conditionally, as local public authorities; central and national public bodies using AI are not named as recipients [inference]. The advice given through these channels is not binding on anyone, and the coders split on two of these passages (one placed 003 and 012 in Delivery/Resources as advice).
themes.holders: Member States (channels), the Commission (sandbox interface), the AI Office (contact for providers of general-purpose AI models). Recipients: SMEs, start-ups, deployers, other innovators, local public authorities, stakeholders, providers.
themes.binding: Art. 62(1)(c) and Art. 57(17) are statutory duties ('shall'), but the reach to local public authorities is qualified by 'as appropriate'; Recital 143 uses 'should'; EU088 is an invitation. No consequence is stated for failing to provide the channels or for not using them.

quotes.quote: utilise existing dedicated channels and where appropriate, establish new ones for communication with SMEs including start-ups, deployers, other innovators and, as appropriate, local public authorities to provide advice and respond to queries about the implementation of this Regulation

The Commission shall develop a single and dedicated interface containing all relevant information related to AI regulatory sandboxes to allow stakeholders to interact with AI regulatory sandboxes and to raise enquiries with competent authorities
invites providers to immediately and proactively contact the AI Office to ensure they are taking the right steps to ensure compliance

themes.theme: Secretariat and support for EU coordination bodies and joint investigations
themes.definition: Administrative, analytical and coordination support that the AI Office or the Commission provides to the European AI Board, its sub-groups and joint investigations.
themes.what_is_set_out: EU046 makes the AI Office the Board's secretariat: it 'shall provide the secretariat for the Board, convene the meetings upon request of the Chair, and prepare the agenda' (Art. 65(8)). The AI Office also 'shall provide coordination support for joint investigations' (Art. 74(11)), a sentence repeated in Recital 160 with 'should'. Recital 149 says the Commission should support the Board's standing subgroup for market surveillance with market evaluations or studies, in particular, per the coder, to identify parts of the Regulation that need specific and urgent coordination. The passages name the support but not its size or form: no staff, budget, time or method is given, and what 'coordination support' for an investigation involves (sharing evidence, testing, analysis) is not stated.
themes.holders: The AI Office (Board secretariat; coordination support for joint investigations); the Commission (market evaluations or studies for the market surveillance subgroup).
themes.binding: The articles use 'shall', a statutory duty on the AI Office; the recitals use 'should', which explains rather than binds. No consequence is stated.
themes.checks: Joint investigations are checks on AI systems by market surveillance authorities [inference from their place in Article 74]. For the support described here: trigger not stated; compared against not stated; metric or threshold not stated; who: the AI Office supports, the investigating authorities are not named in these passages; what happens with the result: not stated.

quotes.quote: The AI Office shall provide the secretariat for the Board, convene the meetings upon request of the Chair, and prepare the agenda
The AI Office shall provide coordination support for joint investigations.
the Commission should support the activities of the standing subgroup for market surveillance by undertaking market evaluations or studies

themes.theme: Competence and knowledge of the people who connect actors
themes.definition: Requirements or expectations that the people who link bodies together (Board representatives, public procurers, data protection officers) have the competence, powers or understanding to do so, and the guidance meant to build that competence.
themes.what_is_set_out: EU046 requires Member States to ensure that their Board representatives 'have the relevant competences and powers in their Member State' to contribute to the Board's tasks (Art. 65(4)(a)); Recital 149 adds that they may be any persons in public entities who should have the competences and powers to facilitate coordination at national level. Neither says which competences. JRC129100 says that even where a national AI strategy is led by the private sector, the public sector must 'ensure that there is enough knowledge to guarantee effective procurement or collaboration', a statement the coder records as hedged ('it may still be very much required'). The EDPS orientations say it is important that DPOs, who advise independently, understand the lifecycle of a generative AI system; the coder notes this includes when and how the system processes personal data and how its input and output mechanisms work. The Omnibus requires the Board to adopt recommendations, taking account of European competence frameworks, that support the Commission and Member States in promoting AI literacy and set common objectives. None of these passages provides training, defines a level of competence or says how it would be checked.
themes.holders: Member States (for their Board representatives); 'the public sector' in countries with private-sector-led strategies; DPOs, with the holder of the duty to ensure their understanding not stated; the European Artificial Intelligence Board (literacy recommendations).
themes.binding: Art. 65(4)(a) is a statutory duty on Member States; Recital 149 uses 'should'. The Omnibus makes adopting recommendations a duty ('shall adopt'), but the recommendations are advisory. JRC129100 is hedged recommendation and the EDPS passage is non-binding interpretation ('it is important to ensure'). No consequence is stated anywhere.

quotes.quote: have the relevant competences and powers in their Member State so as to contribute actively to the achievement of the Board’s tasks referred to in Article 66
ensure that there is enough knowledge to guarantee effective procurement or collaboration

quotes.location: PDF p.15 (printed p.14), s.5 Role of DPOs
quotes.quote: it is important to ensure that DPOs, within their role, advise and assist in an independent manner on the application of the Regulation, have a proper understanding of the lifecycle of the generative AI system

quotes.location: Art. 1(5), replacing AI Act Art. 4(3); p. 16
quotes.quote: The Board shall adopt recommendations, taking into account European competence frameworks, to support the Commission and Member States in the promotion of AI literacy required under paragraph 1, including by setting out common objectives.

themes.theme: Common interpretive guidance and shared frameworks
themes.definition: Guidelines, opinions, recommendations or frameworks issued centrally so that several authorities, or several teams, apply the rules or reason about AI in the same way (closest starting code: shared templates).
themes.what_is_set_out: The Commission's guidelines on the AI Act prohibitions (EU043) aim to give 'insights into the Commission's interpretation' so that Article 5 is applied consistently and uniformly, and, per the coder, ask national market surveillance authorities to draw inspiration from them (para 54). The EDPB opinion (EU074) provides a framework for supervisory authorities to assess specific cases; the coder notes it is linked to an 'utmost account' expectation and to consistent application across the EEA, and is not exhaustive. The Omnibus has the Board adopt recommendations that set common objectives for AI literacy. The JRC report JRC143539 offers its framework as 'a shared language across technical, policy and management perspectives', which the coder reads as coordination within a single administration [inference]. The pull of these texts differs: the EDPB opinion comes with an 'utmost account' expectation (per the coder), the Commission guidelines only invite authorities to 'draw inspiration', and the JRC framework is a discussion aid.
themes.holders: The European Commission (guidelines), with national market surveillance authorities as users; the EDPB (opinion), with competent supervisory authorities as users; the European AI Board (recommendations), with the Commission and Member States as recipients; the JRC report authors (framework), with teams in administrations as users.
themes.binding: All are non-binding interpretation or advice. The guidelines invite authorities to draw inspiration; the EDPB opinion frames rather than decides cases, with an 'utmost account' expectation per the coder; the Board's duty to adopt literacy recommendations is statutory but the recommendations are not; the JRC framework is offered for discussion. No consequence is stated.

quotes.quote: These Guidelines aim to increase legal clarity and to provide insights into the Commission’s interpretation of the prohibitions in Article 5 AI Act with a view to ensuring their consistent, effective and uniform application
This Opinion provides a framework for competent SAs to assess specific cases where (some of) the questions raised in the Request would arise.
The framework as a whole – it offers a shared language across technical, policy and management perspectives

themes.theme: Registers of AI systems and their common vocabulary
themes.definition: Registers or databases that record AI systems or algorithms, and the shared standards needed to make such registers work across bodies.
themes.what_is_set_out: The Commission guidelines on prohibitions (EU043) state that remote biometric identification (RBI) systems used for law enforcement will be registered in a secure non-public section of the database, with limited information and limited access to that information; the coder notes this is the EU database under the AI Act and that its operator is not named. JRC129100 recommends a 'united registry at the EU level' of algorithms, guided by the existing city registers of Amsterdam and Helsinki, and names common standards of vocabulary or ontology as 'a key requirement'; the coder notes it suggests drawing on the INSPIRE federated catalogue. The two documents pull in different directions: the AI Act database withholds law-enforcement entries from public view and limits access, while the JRC recommendation models its registry on municipal registers that are open to the public [inference: the passages do not say the JRC registry would be public]. Neither passage says whether a register entry would hold any information on how a system was tested or how it performs.
themes.holders: Operator of the EU database not stated; the cities of Amsterdam and Helsinki (existing registers); the holder of the proposed EU registry and of its standards not stated.
themes.binding: EU043 describes registration in the future tense ('will be registered') as an arrangement under the AI Act; the JRC passages are recommendation or mention ('A key requirement', 'can provide guidance'). No consequence is stated.

quotes.quote: RBI systems used for the purpose of law enforcement will be registered in a se cure non -public section of the database, with limited information and limited access to that information.
Existing experiences of registries of algorithms, such as those in the cities of Amsterdam and Helsinki, can provide guidance for establishing a united registry at the EU level.
A key requirement for creating an EU -wide registry is also the establishmen t of common standards (vocabulary/ontology)

themes.theme: Shared repositories, platforms and reusable components
themes.definition: Repositories, catalogues, platforms and interoperability frameworks through which public administrations can find use cases, suppliers, standards and AI components, and reuse what other bodies have built.
themes.what_is_set_out: JRC129100 says guidelines are 'needed' to build reusable components on common standards, points to the AI4EU initiative as hosting AI components that can be freely reused (the coder notes the same sentence names the Commission's Connecting Europe Facility, ISA2 interoperability solutions and European Digital Innovation Hubs), and recommends dedicated national repositories of 'standards, guidelines and performance metrics'. JRC143539 names existing or announced Commission offers: Public Sector Tech Watch with examples of AI use cases in public administrations (over 2,000, per the coder), EU GovTech catalogues of start-ups and SMEs, the AI on Demand platform as a collaborative space, and a revised European Interoperability Framework that 'will serve' administrations seeking interoperability by design. The ECA's strategy (ECA_strategy) commits the ECA to keep exploring 'the adoption of solutions created and tested by other institutions', and the coder notes mentions of API access to Commission tools and testing of CJEU tools. The JRC129100 items are proposals with no named holder, the JRC143539 items are existing or forthcoming Commission offers, and the ECA item is a self-commitment. The only reference to measuring tool performance is the JRC129100 call for repositories of 'performance metrics', which does not say what the metrics are or how they would be used.
themes.holders: Not stated for the JRC129100 proposals (guidelines, national repositories); the AI4EU initiative and the European Commission (CEF, ISA2, EDIH) for reusable components; the European Commission for Public Sector Tech Watch, EU GovTech, the AI on Demand platform and the revised EIF; other EU institutions as sources and the ECA as adopter of tested solutions.
themes.binding: JRC129100: 'are needed', 'should be envisaged', i.e. recommendations without holders. JRC143539: descriptions of existing or forthcoming offers ('offers', 'provides', 'will serve'). ECA: 'we will continue to explore'. No consequence is stated.
themes.checks: Only passage 034 touches on checking tools: it proposes repositories of 'performance metrics'. Trigger: not stated; compared against: not stated; metric or threshold: not stated (no metric is named); who: not stated; what happens with the result: not stated. The ECA's 'solutions created and tested by other institutions' implies testing by the originating institution, but the passage does not say how or against what [inference].

quotes.quote: dedicated national repositories of standards, guidelines and performance metrics should be envisaged in combination with the above.
PSTW offers examples of AI use cases in public administrations, and EU GovTech catalogues provide information on European start-ups and SMEs active in the field.

The revised EIF, as announced in the Interoperable Europe Act and referred to in the Apply AI Strategy, will serve as a useful resource, enabling public administrations to embrace an interoperable by design approach.
we will continue to explore the adoption of solutions created and tested by other institutions.

themes.theme: Funding for AI adoption, experimentation and research
themes.definition: Money, grants or financial incentives proposed or reported to support public-sector AI adoption, cross-border experimentation, research and data opening.
themes.what_is_set_out: Every funding passage in this group comes from one document, JRC129100, and none states an amount. It reports the Commission's Adopt AI programme, proposed in the AI White Paper, as set to play 'a crucial role' in strengthening and facilitating AI procurement in the public sector, and a Commission proposal to fund a GovTech Incubator under the Digital Europe Programme for cross-border and cross-domain experimentation. Its own recommendations are to combine international, national, regional and local funding 'in a complementary manner', to earmark funding and grants for dedicated research on AI in the public sector, and to consider 'financial or in-kind benefits' for opening up service data sets. Who would give or receive the money is mostly not stated. None of the funding is tied to testing, evaluating or monitoring AI tools.
themes.holders: The European Commission (Adopt AI programme; GovTech Incubator proposal); otherwise not stated.
themes.binding: Reports of Commission programmes or proposals ('will play', 'has proposed') and suggestions ('Promote', 'it is suggested', 'could be'). No obligation and no consequence. Two coders split on 025 and 028 (one placed them in Delivery/Resources).

quotes.quote: Commission has proposed to fund a GovTech Incubator under the Digital Europe Programme 79 that would enable cross-border and cross-domain experimentation in all related domains.
Promote the use of international funding together with national, regional and local funding in a complementary manner.
it is suggested to earmark funding and grants to support dedicated research in this area

themes.theme: Data availability and open data sharing
themes.definition: Measures to make data, including public service data, more available and shareable between public bodies and others, and the technical standards that support sharing.
themes.what_is_set_out: All passages come from JRC129100 and all are options rather than recommendations. The report says the initiative under the proposed Data Governance Act 'could be explored to enhance data availability also for the public sector' (the coder notes a Board that would support cross-sectoral standardisation and interoperability of high-quality data). It also suggests raising public service officials' awareness of how sharing open data can help society, offering 'financial or in-kind benefits for opening up service data sets', and supporting API frameworks and web standards (the coder notes a footnote pointing to a JRC proposal for a government API framework). The coders flagged three of these passages (029, 030, 031) as scope doubts because they concern open data and interoperability in general rather than AI tools. Nothing in these passages links data sharing to evaluating AI tools, for example through shared test data.
themes.holders: The European Commission (proposed Data Governance Act and associated initiative, per the coder); otherwise not stated; public service officials as the target of awareness-raising.
themes.binding: 'could be explored', 'could be envisaged', 'could be', 'could also be considered'. No obligation and no consequence.

quotes.quote: This initiative could be explored to enhance data availability also for the public sector.
Raise awareness to support a better understanding on the part of public service officials of how sharing open data can assist society
Support to API frameworks73 and web standards could also be considered.

themes.definition: People, networks, fora and partnerships that carry knowledge, advice and shared resources between public bodies, and between public bodies and outside partners.
themes.what_is_set_out: JRC129100 recommends identifying 'AI champions', individuals or organisations per the footnote the coder cites, to raise awareness and to advise and assist local administrations, for instance on coordinating AI procurement and collaborating on upskilling; who identifies them is not stated. JRC143539 says strong support systems and networks, including partnerships, 'can facilitate knowledge sharing and resource pooling', and that collaboration with 'trusted suppliers and partners is essential' to experimentation and adoption, without saying how a supplier comes to be trusted. The ECA commits to share its training material, methodologies and lessons learned and to run practical workshops for the wider community of public sector auditors, and to explore reusing solutions tested by other institutions; per the coder, it also floats making a methodology chatbot available to outside users. AIatEC directs knowledge sharing through established inter-institutional channels and existing Member State fora such as the Network of Member State Chief Information Officers and the Interoperability Expert Group. Only the ECA makes a concrete offer of its own, and it is aimed at public auditors, who may be the ones auditing AI use [inference]; the others are encouragements or pointers to fora that already exist.
themes.holders: AI champions (individuals or organisations), with who appoints them not stated; unnamed administrations building networks and partnerships; trusted suppliers and partners (outside the state); the ECA ('we') offering to public sector auditors; inter-institutional channels, the Network of Member State Chief Information Officers and the Interoperability Expert Group.
themes.binding: Recommended ('it is also recommended'), encouraged ('can facilitate', 'is essential'), self-committed ('We will share') or directed without a holder ('This should use'). No consequence is stated. The coders split on 054 and 055 (one placed them in Coordination/Design) and on 059 (one placed it in Accountability/Resources).

quotes.quote: it is also recommended to identify AI champions 46 who would raise awareness, provide advice and assistance to local administration in a given geographical context and on specific topics (e.g., coordination of AI procurement, collaboration in upskilling, etc.).
Establishing strong support systems and networks, including partnerships with other organisations and stakeholders, can facilitate knowledge sharing and resource pooling.

We will share our training material, methodologies, and lessons learned, and we will organise practical workshops to support the wider community of public sector auditors in navigating the challenges and opportunities presented by AI.

This should use established inter - institutional channels and build on existing Member State cooperation fora su ch as the Network of Member State Chief Information Officers, the Interoperability Expert Group

themes.theme: Information and metrics passed between AI providers and deployers
themes.definition: Documentation, technical information or metrics that AI providers are asked to pass to deployers or integrators, or that a supervisory body supplies so that deployers can ask providers for them.
themes.what_is_set_out: The code of practice EU121 encourages signatories that provide generative AI systems to give deployers and other expert users documentation and other relevant information, excluding confidential business information and trade secrets, so they can make informed decisions; the coder notes this concerns choosing, accessing and interpreting marking and detection solutions. The guidelines on general-purpose AI models (EU088) say that, for the open-source exemption, information about a model's usage should include the technical means (instructions for use, infrastructure, tools) needed to integrate it into AI systems; the coder records a minimum of information on input and output modalities, capabilities and limitations, and infers that the exemption is lost if the information is not made public. The EDPS's AI risk guidance (EDPS_AI_risk) supplies fairness metrics for EU institutions to use when they request metrics from providers: false positive rate parity, under which incorrect positive cases are compared across groups and 'should be similar', and, per the coder, false negative rate parity, calibration fairness and equality of opportunity. The EDPS passage is the only one in this group that names a measure of a tool's outputs. Whether public bodies are among the deployers who receive information under EU121 and EU088 is not stated [inference: they may be].
themes.holders: Signatories who are providers of generative AI systems (EU121); providers of general-purpose AI models released under a free and open-source licence (EU088); the EDPS as source of the metrics, with EU institutions as requesters and providers as the ones who would produce the figures [inference].
themes.binding: EU121: 'encouraged', and proportionate to the signatory's size per the coder. EU088: a condition for an exemption, worded 'should' in non-binding guidelines; the consequence, per the coder's inference, is that the exemption does not apply. EDPS: guidance, with the metric 'should be similar'; no consequence stated.
themes.checks: For the EDPS fairness metrics (044): trigger: not stated in the passage; compared against: the same error rate across different groups of people; metric or threshold: false positive rate parity (and, per the coder, false negative rate parity, calibration fairness and equality of opportunity), with the only threshold being that the rates 'should be similar', and no numeric tolerance; who: the provider produces the figures and the EU institution requests them [inference]; what happens with the result: not stated. Nothing in these passages concerns accuracy against a reference, consistency or repeatability, prompts or configuration, model versions, confidence scores or which cases reach a human. EU121 and EU088 describe information, not checks.

quotes.quote: a. False Positive Rate (FPR) Parity: The number of incorrect positive cases can be compared across different groups. This metric should be similar for these groups.

Signatories are encouraged to ensure that documentation and other relevant information (excluding business confidential information and trade secrets) is provided to deployers and other expert users to support them in making informed decisions
Information about the model’s usage should also include the technical means (e.g. instructions for use, infrastructure, tools) required for the model to be integrated into AI systems

themes.definition: Detection solutions for AI-generated content that providers may use or share, and the expectation that these solutions work with one another.
themes.what_is_set_out: The Commission guidelines on Article 50 (EU_Art50) let a provider of generative AI systems rely on its own detection solution or on a third-party or shared one, 'so long as' it is interoperable with the detection solutions other providers use. The coder notes this applies only where standards are not yet available, especially at the initial stage, and is to be limited in time until harmonised standards exist. The guidelines also refer to publicly available industry-standard detection solutions that let any third party implement detection, 'ideally locally executable on the digital device'; these are resources from non-state actors, named only generically. The passages set no level of detection performance, do not say who checks that detection works, and do not mention public bodies as users of detection [inference: they could fall under 'any third party'].
themes.holders: Providers of generative AI systems; providers of third-party or shared detection solutions; industry standard-setters and providers of publicly available detection solutions.
themes.binding: 'may': a permitted interim option, limited in time per the coder; the second passage is a mention of external solutions. No consequence is stated.
themes.checks: Detection checks whether a piece of content was produced by AI, so it is a check on outputs. Trigger: not stated; compared against: not stated (the marks or signals that providers embed [inference]); metric or threshold: not stated, only interoperability is required; who: the provider, or any third party using a public detection solution; what happens with the result: not stated.

quotes.quote: the provider may rely on its own detection solution or on a third party or shared detection solution , so long as th ose solutions ensure interoperability with the detection solutions used by other providers
publicly-available industry standard detection solution s that allow any third party to implement detection that is ideally locally executable on the digital device

themes.definition: Whether EU and national cybersecurity bodies have enough capacity to coordinate the handling of software vulnerabilities found at scale with the help of frontier AI.
themes.what_is_set_out: ENISA (ENISA_frontier) observes that its own capacity, and that of manufacturers, national CSIRTs and national coordinated disclosure processes, 'may need further reinforcement or reconsideration' to cope with a large wave of newly discovered vulnerabilities, and points to the Cyber Resilience Act's Single Reporting Platform and EU Vulnerability Database as able to help. It does not say who would provide the reinforcement or what it would consist of. The coders treat this as an edge case: AI here is a means of finding vulnerabilities, used by attackers and defenders, rather than a tool used by public officials whose outputs are being governed. It is nonetheless the only passage in this group that says outright that a coordination mechanism may lack capacity.
themes.holders: ENISA; manufacturers; national CSIRTs; national coordinated disclosure processes; operator of the Single Reporting Platform and EU Vulnerability Database not stated.
themes.binding: An observation ('may need') and a statement of possibility ('can help'). No obligation and no consequence.
themes.checks: n/a (the vulnerabilities are in software generally; no check on an AI tool's outputs is described)

quotes.location: Impact on vulnerability and patch management; p. 7
quotes.quote: ENISA’s current capacity, as well as that of manufacturers, national CSIRTs, and national coordinated disclosure processes, may need further reinforcement or reconsideration to manage a large wave of newly discovered vulnerabilities.
The CRA’s Single Reporting Platform (SRP) and EU Vulnerability Database (EUVD) can help support the operationalisation of some of these recommendations.

absences: Of the Coordination starting codes, 'referrals between bodies' has no passages at all: nothing provides resources for passing a case, complaint or finding from one body to another. 'Contact points' appears only as general advice channels and an invitation to providers; no resourced contact point serves public bodies as deployers. Of the Resources starting codes, 'time' has no passages: no deadline, schedule or allocation of time is attached to any coordination resource. Money appears only in one JRC report (JRC129100), with no amounts and mostly no named giver or recipient. Staff appear only as the AI Office's secretariat role and the 'relevant competences' of Board representatives, with no numbers or definitions. Training appears only as the ECA's offer to public auditors and the Board's AI literacy recommendations; nothing trains officials who coordinate the assurance of AI tools. Access appears mainly as a restriction (the non-public section of the EU database). A reader would also expect, and does not find in these passages: model contract terms written for public buyers in a binding text (the AI Act terms cover provider-supplier contracts, and public-procurement clauses appear only as an EDPS example); any shared test data, benchmark, evaluation template or channel through which providers, public bodies and regulators exchange evidence on a tool's accuracy, consistency or repeatability, prompts and configuration, model versions or confidence scores; and any resource for public bodies to report problems with a tool to its provider or to a regulator. The EDPS fairness metrics and the JRC call for repositories of 'performance metrics' are the only points of contact with checking outputs.
cross_cutting: Two kinds of material dominate this cell. EU046 (with its amendment in the Omnibus) provides coordination infrastructure mainly for regulators and market actors: a Board secretariat, support for joint investigations, an electronic notification tool, a sandbox interface and advice channels, mostly as statutory duties ('shall') on the AI Office, the Commission and Member States. The JRC report JRC129100 supplies much of the rest as recommendations or options with no named holder: procurement guidelines, funding, data sharing, AI champions, an EU algorithm registry and repositories. Public bodies that use AI tools are seldom the named recipients of these resources; they appear as 'local public authorities' reached 'as appropriate', as public buyers whose best practice the AI Office must 'promote', as EU institutions advised by the EDPS, and as the auditors the ECA offers to train. Almost nothing is quantified: no money, staff or time is attached to any resource, and competence is left as 'relevant'. On checking AI outputs the cell is close to empty: the only named metric is the EDPS's fairness parity across groups ('should be similar', with no threshold), alongside an unspecified JRC call for repositories of 'performance metrics' and the expectation that detection of AI-generated content be interoperable; nothing is provided for sharing evidence on accuracy, consistency, prompts, model versions or confidence scores between providers, public bodies and regulators. The cell's boundary is soft: for 36 of the 60 passages only one coder placed them here, the other often placing them in Delivery/Resources or Coordination/Design, so the themes rest on contested membership.
